guides.title: Basket or oven-style air fryer: what should you compare?
guides.description: A buyer's guide that starts with how you cook, then tells you what to compare between basket and oven-style air fryers.
guides.deck: Two shapes, two different kitchens. Decide this before you look at a single model number.

body.text: A basket air fryer is a drawer with a heating element and a fan above it. An oven-style air fryer is a small countertop oven that uses the same fast-moving air. They are sold as if they were the same appliance in different clothes. In practice they suit different cooking.
The three questions that actually decide it

items: What is the biggest single thing you cook? A whole chicken or a 12-inch pizza needs a door and a rack, not a drawer.
Do you cook two foods on two different timings? That points at two baskets, or at an oven with two racks and a single shared temperature.
How much counter and cabinet space do you have? A drawer pulls out; French doors open forward. Both need clearance you may not have.

body.text: The two shapes on the tracked products

The figures below are the manufacturers' own published specifications, read on 2026-11-20. They are not test results, and capacity is not comparable across shapes: six quarts of drawer, eight quarts of basket and 26 quarts of oven are three different kinds of space.
Pick the shape, then pick the size

Once the shape is settled, the size question is usually a question about your counter. Measure the depth with the drawer open or the doors swung out, not just the closed footprint. The three tracked appliances need between 10.6 and 14.8 inches of height and between 12.6 and 16.9 inches of depth.
What this guide does not do

It does not tell you which brand is better. It has not tested any of these appliances, and the chefman and Emeril pages on this site say the same. If you want the shape decision in a single table, the comparison page has it.

One thing worth knowing before you shop: on two of the tracked listings the advertised headline disagrees with the manufacturer's own specification sheet. The Chefman 8 Qt listing advertises 450 °F where Chefman publishes 400 °F, and the Chefman 6 Qt listing calls the product an oven where its own page describes a two-drawer basket fryer. Read the maker's specification, not the listing title.

guides.title: A no-hype checklist for comparing air fryer capacity
guides.description: How to read air fryer capacity on a listing, including total quarts versus per-basket quarts, and how to test a load.
guides.deck: Quarts are the number everyone quotes and the number that misleads the most.

body.text: Air fryer capacity is usually given in quarts. That number hides three different things: how much food actually fits in one layer, whether the space is one chamber or several, and whether the quoted figure is usable volume or total volume.
A five-point checklist for any listing

items: Is the capacity one chamber or the sum of several? Two 3-quart baskets are 6 quarts, but you cannot put a 6-quart item in them.
Does the maker give litres as well as quarts? Both of the tracked Chefman pages do, which lets you check the conversion instead of trusting it.
What are the basket's inside dimensions? Quarts say nothing about whether a whole chicken or a pizza fits.
How full can it be loaded? Air frying needs a single layer with room for air to move; the usable capacity is smaller than the marketed one.
Is the outer footprint the same as the cooking area? The 8-quart Chefman is 15.4 in deep; the 6-quart dual basket is 13.38 in deep. Measure the counter, not the capacity.

body.text: The same word, four different sizes

The gap between 6 and 26 quarts is not a gap in quality. It is the difference between cooking two portions at once and cooking for four to six people, which is the range the Emeril page states for its oven.
What to do with the number

Convert it into a meal. If you usually cook for two, ask whether two portions fit in one layer. If you cook for four, ask whether the basket is big enough for all four portions at once or whether you will be cooking in batches. That question is more useful than the quart figure on its own.
Where these numbers came from

Every figure above was read on the manufacturer's own product page on 2026-11-20 and is cited by source id. Where a manufacturer does not publish a value, this site leaves it blank rather than estimating it.

guides.title: How to assess cleanup and counter-space trade-offs
guides.description: A practical way to compare cleanup effort, basket care, and the room a countertop appliance needs.
guides.deck: The appliance you use is the one that is easy to clean and has somewhere to live.

body.text: Two things get decided after the purchase and are rarely discussed before it: where the appliance lives, and how much of it has to be washed. Both are answerable from the manufacturer's published dimensions and materials list.
Measure three things, not one

items: The closed footprint. Every maker publishes this: the tracked appliances range from 13.38 in to 16.9 in deep.
The space it needs to open. A drawer pulls straight out; French doors swing forward. Measure with the appliance open, and check what is above it if the lid or door lifts.
The clearance to the wall and to the cabinet above, which decides whether the heat and steam have anywhere to go. The manufacturer's manual states this; the product page often does not.

body.text: Then count the parts that touch food

headers: Parts that come out to wash
rows: Not stated on the maker's page for each part

body.text: A dual-basket appliance has two of everything, which is twice the washing but also means one basket can soak while the other cooks. An oven has racks and a tray and a door with a gasket and crevices.
The counter-space test, in one minute

Clear the counter space you think you have. Put a sheet of paper down at the footprint of the appliance you are considering, then put a second sheet where the drawer or doors would open. If both fit without moving anything you use daily, the appliance has a home. If you have to move the kettle every time, it does not, and it will end up in a cupboard.
Cleaning questions to ask before you buy

items: Which parts are nonstick, and does the maker say they are dishwasher-safe? Nonstick coatings survive hand-washing longer.
Is there a window, and does it need cleaning inside and out? A window saves opening the drawer but adds a surface.
Where do the crumbs and grease go? A basket with a removable crisper plate is easier to wash than one with a fixed base.
Does the maker publish a cleaning section in the manual? If it does, read it before you buy; it is the most honest description of what the appliance is like to own.

body.text: None of the appliances on this site has been cleaned or used by anyone here. The parts lists above are the manufacturers' own descriptions, cited by source id.

guides.title: Questions to ask before buying a multi-function kitchen appliance
guides.description: Eight plain questions to answer before you buy a multi-function countertop appliance.
guides.deck: A 10-in-1 badge is a list of functions, not a promise that you will use them.

body.text: Multi-function appliances trade specialisation for range. That is a good trade if the functions you need are the ones your routine actually uses, and a bad one if the extra functions are what you pay for and never touch.
Questions that separate the useful functions from the badge

items: Which three functions will you use in a normal week? Write them down before you read any listing.
Does the maker list the functions individually? The tracked Emeril oven names ten: air fry, bake, broil, defrost, dehydrate, grill, proof, reheat, roast and warm.
Do the functions need extra accessories to work? Rotisserie needs a spit; grilling may need a plate sold separately.
Is the preset count consistent? The same Emeril page states 25 presets in its specification tiles and 24 in its description. When a maker disagrees with itself, treat the count as approximate.
Does one function compromise another? A big oven takes longer to preheat for a small batch than a drawer does.

body.text: The badge versus the manual

Every maker's product page is a sales page. The manual is where the limits are stated: what temperature each function reaches, what accessories are required, what must not go in the dishwasher. If a manufacturer publishes the manual as a PDF on the product page, download it before you buy. The tracked products link their manuals where the maker provides one.
One worked example

The Emeril Lagasse French Door AirFryer 360 is sold as a 10-in-1 with 24 or 25 presets, depending on which part of its own page you read. It holds 26 quarts and measures 16.9 in deep by 15.8 in wide by 14.8 in tall. Its maker does not publish a wattage or a temperature range on the product page, so this site does not claim either. That absence is itself a question worth asking before you buy.
If you only ask one question

Ask what the appliance does badly. Every one of them does something badly: a 26-quart oven is slow to heat for a handful of fries, and a drawer with two 3-quart baskets cannot roast a whole chicken. Find that answer before you buy, not after.

guides.title: Is your meat thermometer telling you the right number?
guides.description: The USDA minimum internal temperatures for common meats and poultry, where to place a probe, and what to ask about a wireless thermometer.
guides.deck: A thermometer is only as useful as the number you compare it with.

body.text: The temperatures below are the US Department of Agriculture's published minimum internal temperatures, read from the FSIS chart on 2026-11-20. This guide does not test the accuracy of any thermometer.
The minimum internal temperatures

rows: Beef, pork, veal and lamb steaks, chops and roasts
All poultry: breasts, whole bird, legs, thighs, wings, giblets, stuffing
140 °F (60 °C) if packaged in a USDA-inspected plant, otherwise 165 °F (73.9 °C)

body.text: The USDA adds that these are minimums and that a cook may choose to go higher for personal preference.
Where to put the probe

For a whole bird, the USDA says to check the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing and the thickest part of the breast, avoiding bone. For poultry parts, insert the probe into the thickest area, avoiding bone. Bone heats faster than meat and will give you a reading that is too high.
Instant read or leave in

rows: Taking one reading at the end of cooking
Watching a temperature while food cooks
Not published on the maker's page

body.text: Four questions to ask about any thermometer

items: What range does the manufacturer state, and is it internal or ambient? The CHEF iQ Sense publishes both, and they are very different numbers: 32–212 °F internal against 32–1,000 °F ambient. The higher figure is not a reading range.
How was accuracy established, and is there a certificate? A retail page saying a product is certified is not a certificate. Ask for the accredited laboratory and the certificate number.
Can you calibrate it? The CHEF iQ Sense describes self-calibration with each measurement. An instant-read is usually checked against an ice bath or boiling water; the manual will say how.
What does the app collect? A wireless probe often needs an account and a phone. Read the privacy policy before you connect it to your home network.

body.text: What this site can and cannot tell you

The two tracked thermometers have manufacturer-published specifications on their product pages, cited by source id. Neither has been tested by anyone here, and neither page repeats a certification as fact: the ThermoMaven page quotes ±0.5 °F as the maker's claim and notes that NIST's own FAQ says NIST does not endorse commercial equipment.

note: Guides are written to answer the question in the title, then to hand the reader a way to act on it. Every factual claim names the source it came from. These are working titles informed by the products on the site; they are not claims about search volume (see FLG-034).
